teaching.causalExplanation: The trick is to cut the block into shapes we already know, a rectangle, a triangle or a trapezium. Where you cut matters. Draw a line straight across the block, at right angles to the sides, at the height of the shorter side, thirty metres. Now the block is a rectangle, twenty by thirty, with a triangle sitting on top. The triangle's base is twenty, the width of the block. And its height is forty minus thirty, ten metres. Every piece now has a base and a height we know. Write the plan first. Block equals rectangle plus triangle. Twenty times thirty is six hundred square metres. Half of twenty times ten is a hundred. Together, seven hundred square metres. That's the number for the listing. Here's a good habit. Cut it a different way, and see if you get the same answer. Look at the block as a whole. The left and right sides are parallel, both at right angles to the front, so the whole block is a trapezium. Its parallel sides are forty and thirty, and they're twenty metres apart. A half, times forty plus thirty, times twenty, is seven hundred square metres. Two completely different cuts, and the same answer. That's a strong sign the area is right. And if the two answers don't match, one of the pieces was measured or worked out wrong, so you know to look again. Now the fencing. The front, the left side and the right side are given, but the back fence isn't. Look at the triangle piece again. The back fence is its sloping edge, opposite the right angle. It's a hypotenuse! The two shorter sides are twenty and ten. Twenty squared plus ten squared is five hundred, and the square root is twenty-two point three six metres. The perimeter goes all the way around the outside. Twenty, forty, twenty-two point three six and thirty, a hundred and twelve point three six metres. The cut line we drew is inside the block, so it isn't part of the perimeter. If the front stays open, the fence for the back and sides is ninety-two point three six metres.

scenes.teachingReason: The trick is to cut the block into shapes we already know, a rectangle, a triangle or a trapezium. Where you cut matters. Draw a line straight across the block, at right angles to the sides, at the height of the shorter side, thirty metres. Now the block is a rectangle, twenty by thirty, with a triangle sitting on top. The triangle's base is twenty, the width of the block. And its height is forty minus thirty, ten metres. Every piece now has a base and a height we know. Write the plan first. Block equals rectangle plus triangle. Twenty times thirty is six hundred square metres. Half of twenty times ten is a hundred. Together, seven hundred square metres. That's the number for the listing.

scenes.teachingReason: Rural blocks work the same way, just bigger. This paddock's plan shows a rectangle, a hundred and twenty metres by eighty, with a triangular piece on top. The triangle's base is the same hundred and twenty metres, and its perpendicular height, the dashed line, is forty-five. The rectangle is ninety-six hundred square metres, and the triangle is half of a hundred and twenty times forty-five, twenty-seven hundred. Altogether, twelve thousand three hundred square metres. Land this size is usually given in hectares, and a hectare is ten thousand square metres, so that's one point two three hectares. For the perimeter, the two slanted sides each sit on a right-angled triangle, with the dashed height as one side. The apex is forty metres in from the left, so the right-hand piece is a hundred and twenty minus forty, eighty metres wide. scenes.teachingReason: So how do you choose where to cut? Any cut works, as long as every piece gets a base and a perpendicular height you can read or work out. Try a diagonal cut, corner to corner, as a third check. This triangle has a right angle at the front, so its area is half of twenty times thirty, three hundred square metres. The other one has the forty metre side as its base, and its height is the block's width, twenty, measured at right angles to that side. That's four hundred. Seven hundred again. The slip is a slanted edge used as a height. Half of twenty-two point three six times forty treats the slanted back fence as a height, and that's wrong. Cuts at right angles to a side make the heights easiest to see. Some blocks need more than one cut. An L-shaped block with a slanted corner might need three pieces, and that's fine. More pieces just means more lines in the plan.
